claim: SK-N-AS cells showed repeated oscillations in response to TNFα stimulation that were more damped than those seen in HeLa cells
source: SK-N-AS cells showed repeated oscillations in response to TNFα stimulation that were more damped than those seen in HeLa cells (see Appendix 1—figure 1 for longer time course data [Nelson et al., 2004; Ashall et al., 2009]).
evidence: The claim is supported by references to Appendix 1—figure 1 and citations to previous studies (Nelson et al., 2004; Ashall et al., 2009)

claim: When SK-N-AS cells were treated with a saturating dose of TNFα (10 ng/ml) the initial response of NF-κB was relatively synchronous between cells
source: In previous studies it was observed that when SK-N-AS cells were treated with a saturating dose of TNFα (10 ng/ml) the initial response of NF-κB (i.e. immediate RelA nuclear translocation) was relatively synchronous between cells (Nelson et al., 2004; Ashall et al., 2009; Turner et al., 2010) (Figure 1A; Appendix 1—figure 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Nelson et al., 2004; Ashall et al., 2009; Turner et al., 2010) and references to Figure 1A and Appendix 1—figure 1

claim: SK-N-AS cells treated with 30 pg/ml TNFα showed variation in timing and amplitude even though this was functionally close to a saturating dose
source: However, these data showed a variation in timing and amplitude when cells were treated with a lower dose of 30 pg/ml TNFα, even though this was functionally close to a saturating dose that gave a strong population-level NF-κB response (Turner et al., 2010) (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1B and citation to Turner et al., 2010

claim: HeLa cells showed greater heterogeneity in their initial response at a saturating 10 ng/ml dose of TNFα, with some cells showing little or no response and others showing a variable delay
source: In common with treatment of SK-N-AS cells at 30 pg/ml, HeLa cells showed greater heterogeneity in their initial response at a saturating 10 ng/ml dose of TNFα, with some cells showing little or no response and others showing a variable delay (Nelson et al., 2002; 2004) (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Nelson et al., 2002; 2004 and reference to Figure 1C

claim: HeLa cells showed no significant translocation in response to 30 pg/ml TNFα
source: HeLa cells showed no significant translocation in response to 30 pg/ml TNFα (Figure 1D), suggesting that these cell types have differential dynamic NF-κB responses at varying TNFα doses.
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1D showing experimental data

claim: HeLa cells treated with TNFα in S-phase displayed a reduced nuclear localization of endogenous RelA, compared to those treated in late G1
source: When endogenous RelA was examined using immunocytochemistry, HeLa cells treated with 10 ng/ml TNFα in S-phase displayed a reduced nuclear localization, compared to those treated in late G1 (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunocytochemistry data shown in Figure 1E

claim: Synchronized HeLa cells treated with TNFα in late G1 showed a strong synchronous translocation of RelA, whereas cells treated in S-phase showed reduced RelA translocation
source: These results were confirmed using time-lapse imaging of synchronised HeLa cells transiently transfected with RelA-DsRedxp. Cells treated in late G1 showed a strong synchronous translocation of RelA, whereas cells treated in S-phase showed reduced RelA translocation (Figure 1F,G).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 1F,G

claim: Cell cycle-dependent differences following TNFα treatment were supported by alterations in the extent of IκBα degradation and RelA Serine536 phosphorylation at different stages of the cell cycle
source: These cell cycle-dependent differences following TNFα treatment of synchronized cell populations were supported by alterations in the extent of IκBα degradation and RelA Serine536 phosphorylation at different stages of the cell cycle as measured by western blot (Figure 1H).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1H

claim: HeLa cells treated with TNFα in late G1 (G1/S) showed an increase in the translocation amplitude compared to the unsynchronized population average
source: The resulting data suggested that HeLa cells treated with TNFα in late G1 (inferred to be G1/S) showed an increase in the translocation amplitude compared to the unsynchronized population average (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2C

claim: HeLa cells treated with TNFα in S-phase showed a damped or delayed response with markedly reduced amplitude of nuclear NF-κB translocation
source: By contrast, cells treated in S-phase appeared to show a damped or delayed response (Figure 2C), with markedly reduced amplitude of nuclear NF-κB translocation.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2C

claim: In G2 phase the NF-κB response appeared to be restored
source: In G2 phase the NF-κB response appeared to be restored.
evidence: The claim is based on observations from the experimental data

claim: There was statistically significant higher nuclear translocation amplitude in HeLa cells at G1/S and significantly reduced amplitude in S-phase, compared to G1 and G2
source: Analysis of the complete data set confirmed that there was statistically significant higher nuclear translocation amplitude in HeLa cells at G1/S and significantly reduced amplitude in S-phase, compared to G1 and G2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2

claim: SK-N-AS cells treated with 30 pg/ml TNFα showed a statistically reduced translocation in S-phase compared to G1-phase
source: A smaller data set from SK-N-AS cells treated with 30 pg/ml TNFα, showed once again a statistically reduced translocation in S-phase compared to G1-phase.
evidence: The claim is based on statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: Mean cell cycle duration for HeLa cells treated with TNFα showed a small, but statistically significant increase of 1.9 hr (~10%) compared to untreated cells
source: It was found that mean cell cycle duration for cells treated with TNFα showed a small, but statistically significant increase of 1.9 hr (~10%) compared to untreated cells, with the variability in the total population increasing by ~2-fold (Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 3

claim: HeLa cells treated with TNFα in late G1 had a cell cycle duration that was ~1/3 longer than the untreated population average
source: Within this TNFα-treated population, cells treated in late G1 were more susceptible to cell cycle elongation with a cell cycle duration that was ~1/3 longer than the untreated population average.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of experimental data

claim: TNFα treatment in S-phase had no statistically significant effect on the timing of mitosis
source: TNFα treatment in S-phase had no statistically significant effect on the timing of mitosis.
evidence: The claim is based on statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: In the presence of ectopically-expressed EGFP-E2F-1, there was a reduction in the activity of a NF-κB-regulated luciferase reporter
source: In the presence of ectopically-expressed EGFP-E2F-1, we observed a reduction in the activity of a NF-κB-regulated luciferase reporter (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 4A

claim: The ability of NF-κB to induce endogenous mRNA levels of IκBα and IκBε was impaired in cells co-expressing EGFP-E2F-1 and RelA-DsRedxp, compared to cells expressing RelA-DsRedxp alone
source: Moreover, the ability of NF-κB to induce endogenous mRNA levels of IκBα and IκBε was impaired in cells co-expressing EGFP-E2F-1 and RelA-DsRedxp, compared to cells expressing RelA-DsRedxp alone (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by mRNA level measurements shown in Figure 4B

claim: E2F-1 target gene transcription was impaired by RelA expression, as indicated by a reduction in the activity of a Cyclin E luciferase reporter
source: E2F-1 target gene transcription was also impaired by RelA expression, as indicated by a reduction in the activity of a Cyclin E luciferase reporter (Figure 4C) and in the mRNA level of E2F-1 itself (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 4C

claim: RelA expression reduced the mRNA level of E2F-1
source: E2F-1 target gene transcription was also impaired by RelA expression, as indicated by a reduction in the activity of a Cyclin E luciferase reporter (Figure 4C) and in the mRNA level of E2F-1 itself (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by mRNA level measurements shown in Figure 4D

claim: A predominantly cytoplasmic localization of RelA-DsRedxp was observed when expressed alone, whereas in cells co-expressing EGFP-E2F-1, both proteins were predominantly nuclear
source: In transient transfection experiments, a predominantly cytoplasmic localization of RelA-DsRedxp was observed when expressed alone, whereas in cells co-expressing EGFP-E2F-1, both proteins were predominantly nuclear (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4E

claim: The steady-state cytoplasmic localisation of RelA was restored in cells transiently expressing IκBα-AmCyan in addition to EGFP-E2F-1 and RelA-dsRedxp
source: In addition we also found that the steady-state cytoplasmic localisation of RelA was restored in cells transiently expressing IκBα-AmCyan in addition to EGFP-E2F-1 and RelA-dsRedxp.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations

claim: A decrease in EGFP-E2F-1 expression over time was associated with a re-localization of RelA-DsRedxp from the nucleus to the cytoplasm in both SK-N-AS and HeLa cells
source: Time-series experiments in both SK-N-AS and HeLa cells showed that a decrease in EGFP-E2F-1 expression over time was associated with a re-localization of RelA-DsRedxp from the nucleus to the cytoplasm (for SK-N-AS cells, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–B; for HeLa cells, Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-series imaging data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–B and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–C

claim: There was a strong correlation between the EGFP-E2F-1 decay half-life and the delay in RelA-DsRedxp translocation back into the cytoplasm
source: Quantitative analysis showed a strong correlation between the EGFP-E2F-1 decay half-life and the delay in RelA-DsRedxp translocation back into the cytoplasm (for SK-N-AS cells, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C; for HeLa cells, Figure 4—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and Figure 4—figure supplement 2D

claim: A clear physical interaction between fluorescently labelled E2F-1 and RelA in the nucleus of living cells was evident using Förster Resonance Energy Transfer (FRET)
source: A clear physical interaction between fluorescently labelled E2F-1 and RelA in the nucleus of living cells was evident using Förster Resonance Energy Transfer (FRET), in conjunction with acceptor photobleaching as a qualitative indicator of intermolecular interaction (Figure 5D), and Fluorescence Cross-Correlation Spectroscopy (FCCS) (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by FRET data shown in Figure 5D and FCCS data shown in Figure 5C

claim: Co-immunoprecipitation confirmed a physical interaction between E2F-1 and RelA in HeLa cells synchronized in late G1
source: In order to further support the interaction between the endogenous proteins, we used co-immunoprecipitation (Co-IP) of endogenous E2F-1 and RelA in HeLa cells that had been synchronized in late G1, when E2F-1 levels were at their peak (Figure 5B). These data confirmed a physical interaction between E2F-1 and RelA, in agreement with previous studies (Tanaka et al., 2002; Lim et al., 2007; Garber et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by Co-IP data shown in Figure 5B and citations to previous studies (Tanaka et al., 2002; Lim et al., 2007; Garber et al., 2012)

claim: No positive co-IP between E2F-1 and RelA was observed in asynchronous cells
source: We were not able to observe a positive co-IP in asynchronous cells (see Appendix 1—figure 4), suggesting that this interaction was only detectable in HeLa cells at G1/S when E2F-1 was at its highest level.
evidence: The claim is supported by negative Co-IP results shown in Appendix 1—figure 4

claim: In cells expressing RelA-DsRedxp and EGFP-E2F-1, there was a delay before the onset of oscillations following TNFα stimulation
source: In contrast, time-lapse live cell imaging of SK-N-AS cells stimulated with TNFα, showed that in cells expressing RelA-DsRedxp and EGFP-E2F-1 (which initially had nuclear RelA-DsRedxp), there was a delay before the onset of oscillations (Figure 6B and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 6B and D

claim: The length of the refractory period in cells expressing RelA-DsRedxp and EGFP-E2F-1 was on average ~4-fold longer than the peak1:peak2 timing in cells expressing RelA-DsRedxp alone
source: The length of this refractory period was on average ~4-fold longer than the peak1:peak2 timing in cells expressing RelA-DsRedxp alone (Figure 6B and [Ashall et al., 2009]).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6B and citation to Ashall et al., 2009

claim: TNFα treatment of SK-N-AS cell populations transiently expressing EGFP-E2F-1 and RelA-DsRedxp led to reduced levels of phospho-S536-RelA and stabilized levels of IκBα
source: In support of this prediction, TNFα treatment of SK-N-AS cell populations transiently expressing EGFP-E2F-1 and RelA-DsRedxp led to reduced levels of phospho-S536-RelA and stabilized levels of IκBα (Figure 6E).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6E

claim: Ectopic expression of E2F-1 in cells resulted in increased E2F-4 expression, consistent with E2F-4 being a transcriptional target of E2F-1
source: We confirmed that ectopic expression of E2F-1 in cells resulted in increased E2F-4 expression, consistent with E2F-4 being a transcriptional target of E2F-1 in these cells (Figure 6E).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6E

claim: The profile of E2F-4 expression was delayed relative to that of E2F-1 in the cell cycle, peaking in S-phase in synchronized HeLa cells
source: The profile of E2F-4 expression was found to be delayed relative to that of E2F-1 in the cell cycle, peaking in S-phase in synchronized HeLa cells (Figure 6F).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6F

claim: When transiently expressed in either HeLa or SK-N-AS cells, both E2F-4 and RelA proteins were located in the cytoplasm
source: When transiently expressed in either HeLa or SK-N-AS cells, both proteins were located in the cytoplasm (Figure 7A).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 7A

claim: Following TNFα treatment, the timing of RelA-DsRedxp translocation to the nucleus was delayed relative to the level of the fluorescent signal from EGFP-E2F-4
source: Following TNFα treatment, the timing of RelA-DsRedxp translocation to the nucleus in both cell lines was delayed relative to the level of the fluorescent signal from EGFP-E2F-4 (Figure 7B for dynamic profiles and Figure 7—figure supplement 1 for analysis).
evidence: The claim is supported by dynamic profile data shown in Figure 7B and analysis in Figure 7—figure supplement 1

claim: The physical interaction of endogenous E2F-4 and RelA proteins was supported by Co-IP from HeLa cells synchronized in S-phase
source: The physical interaction of endogenous E2F-4 and RelA proteins was supported by Co-IP from HeLa cells synchronized in S-phase (Figure 7C).
evidence: The claim is supported by Co-IP data shown in Figure 7C

claim: No pull-down of E2F-4 and RelA was observed in cells synchronised in late G1 phase
source: No pull-down was observed in cells synchronised in late G1 phase (see Appendix 1—figure 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by negative Co-IP results shown in Appendix 1—figure 4

claim: The interaction between E2F-4 and RelA was confirmed by acceptor photo bleaching FRET and FCCS data
source: This interaction was confirmed by acceptor photo bleaching FRET and FCCS data obtained from cells transiently expressing ECFP-E2F-4 and RelA-EYFP (for FRET) or RelA-dsRedxp and EGFP-E2F-4 (for FCCS) fluorescent fusion proteins (Figure 7D and E respectively).
evidence: The claim is supported by FRET data shown in Figure 7D and FCCS data shown in Figure 7E

claim: Stable HeLa cell lines with integrated Bacterial Artificial Chromosomes expressing E2F-1-Venus and RelA-DsRedxp showed the same pattern of synthesis and degradation of a transiently expressed FUCCI reporter for SCF (SKP-2) activity, indicating normal cell cycle progression
source: Stable cell lines were generated with a human E2F-1-Venus BAC construct, and showed the same pattern of synthesis and degradation of a transiently expressed FUCCI reporter for SCF (SKP-2) activity, indicating normal cell cycle progression (see Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by FUCCI reporter data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1

claim: All viable clones of E2F-1-Venus BAC had relatively low expression of the E2F-1-Venus BAC, suggesting that E2F-1 over-expression was detrimental to cell survival
source: All viable clones had relatively low expression of the E2F-1-Venus BAC, further suggesting that E2F-1 over-expression was detrimental to cell survival.
evidence: The claim is based on observations during clonal selection and inference about cell survival

claim: The dual BAC stable clonal cell line C1-1 showed a slight increase (~8%) in mean cell cycle length comparable with wild type HeLa
source: This clonal cell line showed a slight increase (~8%) in mean cell cycle length (with similar cell-to-cell variability) comparable with wild type HeLa (see Appendix 1—figure 7).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell cycle timing data shown in Appendix 1—figure 7

claim: TNFα treatment in the C1-1 cell line increased the variability in cell cycle timing compared to that of resting cells
source: Similar to wild type cells, TNFα treatment in the C1-1 cell line increased the variability in cell cycle timing compared to that of resting cells.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of cell cycle timing data

claim: In the dual BAC stable cells, cells treated in late G1/S-phase showed higher amplitude RelA nuclear translocations
source: In agreement with data from the transiently transfected HeLa and SK-N-AS cells (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplements 2 and 3), the cells treated in late G1/S-phase showed higher amplitude RelA nuclear translocations, whereas Cells treated in S-phase showed a statistically significant suppression in S-phase RelA translocation compared to cells in early G1- or G2-phases (Figure 8 and Figure 8—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8 and Figure 8—figure supplement 3, and comparison to previous data in Figure 2

claim: Cells treated in S-phase showed a statistically significant suppression in S-phase RelA translocation compared to cells in early G1- or G2-phases in the dual BAC stable cells
source: In agreement with data from the transiently transfected HeLa and SK-N-AS cells (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplements 2 and 3), the cells treated in late G1/S-phase showed higher amplitude RelA nuclear translocations, whereas Cells treated in S-phase showed a statistically significant suppression in S-phase RelA translocation compared to cells in early G1- or G2-phases (Figure 8 and Figure 8—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 8 and Figure 8—figure supplement 3

claim: FCS analysis estimated 310,000 ± 120,000 molecules of RelA-DsRedxp per cell in the stable cell line
source: Expression of the RelA-DsRedxp and E2F-1-Venus fusion proteins in the stable cell line was quantified through molecular counting of fluorophores via FCS (Figure 8—figure supplement 4). This gave an estimate of 310,000 ± 120,000 molcules of RelA-DsRedxp per cell.
evidence: The claim is supported by FCS measurements shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 4

claim: FCS analysis estimated 24,000 ± 9100 molecules of E2F-1-Venus per cell in the stable cell line
source: By contrast, FCS analysis suggested that E2F-1-Venus expression was lower (24,000 ± 9100 molecules of E2F-1-Venus per cell).
evidence: The claim is based on FCS measurements

claim: RelA showed an approximate ratio of 3:1 ectopic to endogenous expression based on quantitative analysis of western blot data
source: RelA showed an approximate ratio of 3:1 ectopic to endogenous expression based on quantitative analysis of western blot data (see Figure 8—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot analysis shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 4A

claim: Western blot analysis suggested that there was an approximate ratio of 10:1 endogenous to ectopic E2F-1 levels
source: Western blot analysis (Figure 8—figure supplement 4B) suggested that there was an approximate ratio of 10:1 endogenous to ectopic levels).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot analysis shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 4B

claim: A strong cross-correlation between E2F-1-Venus and RelA-DsRedxp was confirmed in the nucleus by FCCS following TNFα stimulation
source: The interaction between E2F-1-Venus and RelA-DsRedxp following TNFα stimulation was measured by Fluorescence Cross-Correlation Spectroscopy (FCCS). A strong cross-correlation was confirmed in the nucleus (Figure 8—figure supplement 4D) indicating that the interaction uncovered by transient transfection with plasmids was not an artefact of over-expression, but was contextually relevant in relation to the cell cycle and RelA activation.
evidence: The claim is supported by FCCS data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 4D

claim: The dissociation constant (Kd) for the RelA-DsRedxp and E2F-1-Venus binding in the nucleus of TNFα–stimulated cells was 12 nM
source: Analysis of the dissociation constant (by FCCS) for the RelA-DsRedxp and E2F-1-Venus binding in the nucleus of TNFα–stimulated cells suggested a dissociation constant (Kd) of 12 nM (Figure 8E).
evidence: The claim is supported by FCCS analysis shown in Figure 8E

claim: TNFα stimulation in S-phase showed a suppressed and delayed translocation of RelA, with no observable perturbation to cell cycle timing
source: TNFα stimulation in S-phase showed a suppressed and delayed translocation of RelA, with no observable perturbation to cell cycle timing.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations from multiple figures

claim: Stimulation in late G1 showed strong translocation of RelA and led to significant lengthening of the cell cycle
source: In contrast, stimulation in late G1 showed strong translocation of RelA (Figure 2) and led to significant lengthening of the cell cycle (Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 3

claim: NF-κB is an important signalling system, implicated in many diseases including autoimmune diseases and cancer
source: Nuclear Factor kappa B (NF-κB) is an important signalling system, implicated in many diseases including autoimmune diseases and cancer (Grivennikov et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Grivennikov et al., 2010

claim: Inflammatory cues such as Tumour Necrosis Factor alpha (TNFα) can trigger the nuclear translocation of the NF-κB RelA subunit and activation of target gene transcription
source: Inflammatory cues such as Tumour Necrosis Factor alpha (TNFα) can trigger the nuclear translocation of the NF-κB RelA subunit and activation of target gene transcription (Hayden and Ghosh, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Hayden and Ghosh, 2008

claim: Nuclear NF-κB activates feedback regulators, including the inhibitory kappa B alpha (IκBα) and epsilon (IκBε) inhibitors
source: Nuclear NF-κB activates feedback regulators, including the inhibitory kappa B alpha (IκBα) and epsilon (IκBε) inhibitors (Arenzana-Seisdedos et al., 1997; Kearns et al., 2006; Paszek et al., 2010), which bind and transport NF-κB back into the cytoplasm.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Arenzana-Seisdedos et al., 1997; Kearns et al., 2006; Paszek et al., 2010

claim: In response to TNFα, the NF-κB system shows nuclear-cytoplasmic (N:C) oscillations in the localization of the NF-κB complex associated with out-of-phase cycles of degradation and re-synthesis of IκB proteins
source: In response to TNFα, this system shows nuclear-cytoplasmic (N:C) oscillations in the localization of the NF-κB complex associated with out-of-phase cycles of degradation and re-synthesis of IκB proteins (Nelson et al., 2004; Ashall et al., 2009; Lee et al., 2009; Sung et al., 2009; Tay et al., 2010; Turner et al., 2010; Ruland, 2011; Hughey et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Nelson et al., 2004; Ashall et al., 2009; Lee et al., 2009; Sung et al., 2009; Tay et al., 2010; Turner et al., 2010; Ruland, 2011; Hughey et al., 2015

claim: The frequency of NF-κB oscillations has been proposed to be a key parameter that regulates the pattern of downstream gene expression
source: Through systems biology and experimental approaches, the frequency of these oscillations has been proposed to be a key parameter that regulates the pattern of downstream gene expression (Ashall et al., 2009; Lee et al., 2014; Williams et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ashall et al., 2009; Lee et al., 2014; Williams et al., 2014

claim: Many NF-κB family members have been characterised as oncoproteins (e.g. c-Rel and Bcl-3)
source: Many NF-κB family members have been characterised as oncoproteins (e.g. c-Rel and Bcl-3 [Hayden and Ghosh, 2008]).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Hayden and Ghosh, 2008

claim: A number of cell cycle control proteins have been shown to be NF-κB transcriptional targets, including Cyclin D
source: Also, a number of cell cycle control proteins have been shown to be NF-κB transcriptional targets, including Cyclin D, (Guttridge et al., 1999; Sée et al., 2004) and p21, an inhibitor of Cyclin Dependent Kinase (CDK) activity (Hinata et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Guttridge et al., 1999; Sée et al., 2004

claim: p21 is an inhibitor of Cyclin Dependent Kinase (CDK) activity and is a NF-κB transcriptional target
source: Also, a number of cell cycle control proteins have been shown to be NF-κB transcriptional targets, including Cyclin D, (Guttridge et al., 1999; Sée et al., 2004) and p21, an inhibitor of Cyclin Dependent Kinase (CDK) activity (Hinata et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Hinata et al., 2003

claim: The E2 Factor (E2F) proteins are differentially expressed during the cell cycle to control cell proliferation
source: The E2 Factor (E2F) proteins are differentially expressed during the cell cycle to control cell proliferation (Bertoli et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Bertoli et al., 2013

claim: E2F proteins are a family of transcription factors that play a key role in the G1/S cell cycle checkpoint
source: They are a family of transcription factors that play a key role in the G1/S cell cycle checkpoint.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about E2F proteins

claim: Previous studies have provided preliminary evidence for physical interaction between NF-κB and E2F proteins
source: Previous studies have provided preliminary evidence for physical interaction between NF-κB and E2F proteins (Tanaka et al., 2002; Lim et al., 2007; Garber et al., 2012)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Tanaka et al., 2002; Lim et al., 2007; Garber et al., 2012

claim: Cells use the G1/S checkpoint to prioritize between inflammatory signalling and the onset of DNA replication prior to cell division
source: These data suggest that cells use the G1/S checkpoint to prioritize between inflammatory signalling and the onset of DNA replication prior to cell division (see schematic diagram in Figure 9).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data and supported by schematic in Figure 9

claim: An inflammatory response during DNA replication might be detrimental to the cell
source: The presence of a mechanism for prioritization between the important processes of cell proliferation and inflammation suggests that an inflammatory response during DNA replication might be detrimental to the cell.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observed prioritization mechanism

claim: Transient exogenous expression of E2F-1 fusion protein (but not E2F-4) alone caused apoptosis, but this was rescued by co-expression of RelA
source: An additional complication in these experiments was that exogenous expression of E2F-1 (but not E2F-4) fluorescent fusion protein from a CMV promoter caused apoptosis when transfected alone. Interestingly this effect was rescued by co-expression with RelA.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations during transfection experiments

claim: E2F-1 and IκBα may compete for binding to RelA
source: We provide some data that suggests that E2F-1 and IκBα may compete for binding to RelA (see Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4E

claim: E2F-1 and RelA are common transcription factor pairs that were bound together at a large set of functionally important gene promoters in dendritic cells following LPS stimulation
source: In support of this, Garber et al. performed a study in dendritic cells where they studied a panel of transcription factors by ChIP-Seq following LPS stimulation. Their data suggested that E2F-1 and RelA are common transcription factor pairs that were bound together at a large set of functionally important gene promoters (see data in Figure 3B of Garber et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Garber et al., 2012

claim: Knock-down of E2F-4 was found to be lethal to cells
source: However, knock-down of E2F-4 was found to be lethal to cells (Crosby and Almasan, 2004) preventing time lapse analysis.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Crosby and Almasan, 2004
